stage.name: What is the OpenHW Foundation?
stage.description: A source-checked map of RISC-V standards, Eclipse governance, OpenHW programme direction, CORE-V IP, and project repositories.

content.title: One ecosystem, five different engineering layers
content.subtitle: Separate the RISC-V standard, Eclipse governance, OpenHW collaboration, CORE-V processor IP, and the repositories that ship the work.
content.thesis: OpenHW does not define the RISC-V ISA. It organises member-driven work around open processor IP and related assets inside the Eclipse governance framework.
content.narration: OpenHW sits in an ecosystem where similar names label different objects. RISC-V International maintains the ISA standard. Eclipse Foundation provides the legal, governance, IP, and collaboration framework. The OpenHW Foundation working group aligns members on strategy, roadmaps, engineering policy, and ecosystem programmes. CORE-V names processor families, while repositories contain concrete artifacts. This lesson separates the layers and routes each question to the right source.

scenes.title: Map each name to one responsibility

content.sceneTitle: Map each name to one responsibility
content.title: These layers cooperate; they are not one command chain
content.subtitle: Use each layer for the decision it is authoritative enough to support.

cards.label: STANDARD
cards.title: RISC-V International
cards.body: Develops, ratifies, and maintains the open RISC-V ISA specifications and related standards.

cards.label: HOST + PROCESS
cards.title: Eclipse Foundation
cards.body: Provides the working-group and project processes, legal/IP framework, infrastructure, and vendor-neutral governance.

cards.label: COLLABORATION
cards.title: OpenHW Foundation
cards.body: A member-driven Eclipse Working Group for strategy, roadmap, funding, branded releases, and the open-hardware ecosystem.

cards.label: ENGINEERING OUTPUT
cards.title: CORE-V projects and repositories
cards.body: Processor RTL, verification, documentation, software, integration material, issues, releases, and contribution history.

content.narration: Do not read this as a corporate hierarchy. RISC-V International is a separate standards organisation, not OpenHW’s parent. Eclipse hosts the OpenHW working group and supplies its governance framework. Members coordinate strategy, investment, roadmaps, and engineering policy. Project communities build artifacts under project governance. CORE-V is a portfolio label, not an organisation. Use RISC-V sources for ISA meaning, the charter for governance, and project docs and releases for implementation behavior.

scenes.title: A standard is not a processor core

content.sceneTitle: A standard is not a processor core
content.title: The ISA defines the contract; a core makes design choices
content.subtitle: Two processors can implement the same RISC-V ISA while using very different microarchitectures.

columns.label: RISC-V SPECIFICATIONS
columns.title: Architectural contract
bullets: Base ISA, extensions, privilege, debug, and related specifications
Developed and ratified through RISC-V International
Does not prescribe one pipeline, cache, predictor, or RTL code base

columns.label: OPENHW PROCESSOR IP
columns.title: Concrete implementation
bullets: Pipeline, issue, cache, interface, and integration decisions
Verification environments, documentation, software, and releases
Examples include the CVA6 and CVE2 code bases

anchor.label: ENGINEERING TEST
anchor.text: “Is this instruction legal?” is a specification question. “How many stages, which interface, and which release?” is a project question.

content.narration: The cleanest boundary is specification versus implementation. A RISC-V specification defines software-visible behavior: encodings, state, privilege rules, and other contracts. It does not force one pipeline or cache. OpenHW projects make those choices. CVE2 is a small two-stage embedded design; CVA6 is a configurable six-stage code base. For instructions and architectural behavior, start with RISC-V specifications. For timing, interfaces, configuration, or release status, use the project manual and repository.

scenes.title: Governance has four separate responsibility zones

content.sceneTitle: Governance has four separate responsibility zones
content.title: Strategy, technical coordination, and project decisions are not the same vote
content.subtitle: The current charter and Eclipse Working Group Process define explicit boundaries.

rows.primaryRole: Host, governance processes, legal/IP, infrastructure and programme support
rows.engineeringSignal: Defines the common process in which the working group and projects operate
rows.boundary: It is not a processor family or ISA owner

rows.primaryRole: Working-group strategy, scope, roadmap, programme plan and budget
rows.engineeringSignal: Approves the direction and which Eclipse projects are in scope
rows.boundary: Strategy is not day-to-day patch approval

rows.primaryRole: Project recommendations, roadmap process, coordination and engineering policy
rows.engineeringSignal: Sets policies for OpenHW-branded releases and cross-project planning
rows.boundary: A TAC policy is not the same as a repository commit

rows.primaryRole: Develop, review, release and maintain concrete code and documentation
rows.engineeringSignal: Committers, issues, reviews, test results, tags and releases carry evidence
rows.boundary: Working groups influence and support; they do not directly manage projects

content.note: The public brand “OpenHW Foundation” and the charter term “OpenHW Foundation Working Group” refer to the same working group.
content.narration: The Drive source points to a Steering Committee and a Technical Advisory Committee; the current charter sets the boundary. The Steering Committee owns working-group strategy, scope, programme plan, roadmap, and budget. The TAC recommends projects, coordinates releases, and defines policies for OpenHW-branded releases. Projects still make project-level decisions through their communities. Eclipse says a working group may guide and support projects, but does not direct or manage them.

content.title: From ecosystem need to a reviewable release
content.subtitle: This is a source-backed mental model, not a mandatory stage-gate for every project.

steps.title: Requirements
steps.body: Members and project communities surface market, architecture, quality, and ecosystem needs.

steps.title: Programme direction
steps.body: The Steering Committee aligns scope, strategy, programme plan, roadmap, and funding.

steps.title: Technical coordination
steps.body: The TAC builds roadmap consensus and defines coordination and branded-release policies.

steps.title: Project work
steps.body: Project contributors design, review, verify, document, and maintain the implementation.

steps.title: Evidence
steps.body: Repositories, tests, documentation, tags, and releases let users inspect the result.

content.takeaway: The working group aligns investment and quality expectations; project evidence determines what can actually be integrated.
content.narration: A useful engineering model starts with needs and ends with evidence. Members and project communities surface requirements. The Steering Committee aligns programme and funding. The TAC coordinates roadmaps and policies. Project communities design, review, verify, document, and maintain the implementation. Users inspect repositories, tests, manuals, tags, and releases. This is a conceptual loop, not a mandatory stage-gate. It preserves the boundary between working-group coordination and project decisions.

scenes.title: OpenHW is more than a directory of CPU RTL

content.sceneTitle: OpenHW is more than a directory of CPU RTL
content.title: A usable processor needs evidence above and below the RTL
content.subtitle: The 2025 Drive deck emphasises a stack; the current project catalog supplies concrete examples.

cards.label: PROCESSOR IP
cards.title: Cores and configurations
cards.body: CVA6 and CVE2 show how a family or code base becomes specific processor configurations.

cards.label: VERIFICATION
cards.title: Testbenches and reusable flows
cards.body: CORE-V-VERIF provides environments and reusable verification assets around CORE-V processors.

cards.label: DOCUMENTATION
cards.title: Specifications and integration guides
cards.body: User manuals, design documents, interface chapters, requirements, and release notes define usable scope.

cards.label: SOFTWARE + SYSTEM
cards.title: Toolchain and platform enablement
cards.body: Software support, examples, FPGA or SoC integration material can connect RTL to a running system.

cards.label: RELEASE EVIDENCE
cards.title: Tags, issues, CI and provenance
cards.body: The repository records what changed, what was tested, which baseline was released, and who reviewed it.

cards.label: PROGRAMME MATERIAL
cards.title: Roadmaps and engineering policy
cards.body: Working-group material coordinates priorities and quality expectations across participating projects.

content.narration: The strongest idea in the Drive material is that OpenHW deliverables form a stack. Processor RTL is only the center. Verification creates repeatable checks. Documentation defines configuration and integration boundaries. Software and platform material connect the processor to a system. Repository history, CI, issues, tags, and releases create provenance. Roadmaps and policy coordinate expectations. Contents differ by project, so use the stack as a checklist and verify every item in current sources.

actions.text: Use the evidence router as a professional habit. A RISC-V specification proves architectural behavior, not the CVA6 pipeline. The charter proves governance, not that a branch passes CI. A TAC roadmap expresses direction, not that planned RTL shipped. A CVA6 repository exposes code and releases, but does not define all RISC-V processors. A CVE2 manual is implementation-specific. CORE-V-VERIF shows a verification environment, not universal coverage. Match every claim to the source scope.

questions.question: Which organisation develops and ratifies the RISC-V ISA specifications?
questions.analysis: RISC-V International is the standards body. OpenHW projects implement and verify processors that conform to relevant RISC-V specifications.

questions.question: What is the OpenHW Foundation in its current charter?
questions.analysis: Charter v1.1 states that OpenHW Foundation is operated as an Eclipse Foundation Working Group and that the two names are interchangeable in that document.

questions.question: Which statement best describes the working-group/project boundary?

options.label: The working group provides strategy, support, and influence; project communities retain project governance
The working group can merge any patch into any project
Projects ratify the RISC-V ISA for RISC-V International
Repositories vote on the working-group budget

questions.analysis: The Eclipse Working Group Process says working groups complement and influence projects but do not direct or manage them.

questions.question: Which items can be OpenHW engineering outputs or project artifacts?

options.label: Processor RTL such as CVA6 or CVE2
Documentation, software, integration assets, and releases
Ratification of the base RISC-V ISA

questions.analysis: OpenHW work can span processor IP and the assets needed to verify and use it. RISC-V International owns ISA specification ratification.

actions.text: The checkpoint tests the boundaries that matter in real work. Identify RISC-V International as the standards body. Recognise OpenHW Foundation as an Eclipse Foundation Working Group. Preserve the boundary between working-group influence and project governance. Finally, identify processor RTL, verification, documentation, software, integration assets, and releases as possible OpenHW outputs, while leaving ISA ratification with RISC-V International.

content.title: Name the layer before trusting the claim
takeaways: RISC-V International defines and ratifies the ISA specifications.
Eclipse Foundation hosts the governance and collaboration framework.
OpenHW aligns strategy, roadmap, policy, funding, and ecosystem work.
Projects and repositories carry implementation, verification, documentation, and release evidence.
